Stating these in text the Agent receives whenever it is pointed at the roster satisfies this; no tool is required.

section.t: The roster's shape is pinned by its schema () and by the roster-* fixtures (). The envelope is Runtime-authored and therefore open (): a consumer ignores members it does not recognize, and emitting one remains producer non-conformance.

section.name: The Peer-Origin Profile (Optional)
section.t: This section is an optional profile. It gives agent-to-agent traffic between Agents of the same principal its own inbound tree, peer/, and states what that tree asserts, who may write it, how peers are addressed, how a reply is correlated with the message it answers, and how peer traffic is carried and verified between hosts. A deployment that implements the profile is bound by every requirement in this section; a deployment that does not is unaffected. No schema or fixture outside the profile depends on it, and the wire contract_version is the same for both.

section.name: Scope
section.t: The profile is optional because peer origin is needed by deployments in which Agents task one another, and by no deployment that only handles mail.

The tree is named for what it asserts, not for what it is used for: peer/ asserts authenticated, same-principal peer origin, and the document kind is peer. What a Connector does with a peer message (delegation, review, notification) is the Connector's business. Because the kind and the tree share a name, the rule that a document's kind equals the name of the tree it was read from is mechanical.

The profile adds an origin class and reuses mail threading for correlation. It defines no call or return semantics, no method or operation member, and no status vocabulary for the work itself: a reply is prose authored by an Agent, with the posture of any other peer content. This keeps the profile on the mail side of the line drawn in .

The profile relies on two generic rules in : the tree rules (every Runtime-owned inbound-class tree is an origin class, derived from the tree and never from a member, with notice_id uniqueness, content_ref confinement and write authority all per tree), and the outbound extension space outbound/ext/<name>/, where delivery outcomes are kept (). There is deliberately no inbound extension space.

section.name: The Peer Tree

figure.name: Namespace layout with the peer tree (illustrative — not a fixture)
figure.sourcecode: <agent-id>/ outbound/ # as in the Volume Layout inbound/ # mail notices/ messages/ peer/ # PROFILE: same layout, conventions notices/notice-<id>.json # and Sidecar rules as inbound/ notices/<notice-id>.attachments/<i> messages/notice-<id>.json audit/

section.t: A sibling of inbound/, never a child. Nesting the peer tree inside the mail tree would put the tree the mail deliverer must not write inside the tree it must write, so the write-authority partition () would have to be carved out of a mount instead of being one. As a sibling, the partition coincides with mount granularity. Every obligation on inbound/ in applies to peer/ unchanged: it is Runtime-owned; it MAY be mounted read-only; a Connector MUST NOT require write access to it; only the Runtime deletes from it; and its retention is conservative and age-based.

Its own schema. A Peer Notice is pinned by the peer-notice schema (): the Deliver Notice shape with kind fixed to "peer" and message.mailbox fixed to "peer", message.from pinned to a bare addr-spec (), message.id, message.in_reply_to and message.references[] pinned to the notice_id character set (), and the optional Runtime-asserted message.sender_exposure (). Attachment Descriptors are exactly those of . The body spool uses the Inbound Message schema () unchanged. Because a Peer Notice appears only in a tree that a mail-only consumer never reads, the closed kind vocabulary of the Deliver Notice is untouched.
The cross-lock. A deliver document under peer/notices/ fails the peer-notice schema, and a peer document under inbound/notices/ fails the Deliver Notice schema. Both are dropped under the rule of .

The placer mints notice_id. The component that places a notice into a tree mints its notice_id. Where a tree has more than one writer, each MUST mint so that a collision between writers is negligible: at least 128 bits of entropy under the notice_id character set, or a writer-specific prefix. A consumer that keys state across trees MUST include the tree in the key. On a single host, a Runtime MAY make the notice_id equal to the peer message id (). Between hosts they differ, because the receiving Runtime mints the notice_id and the message id is the sender's. A consumer MUST NOT assume that they coincide.

content_ref is confined to its tree. Bytes resolve only within the notices/ directory of the tree the enclosing document was read from, recomputed from that document's notice_id and the Descriptor's index. A Peer Notice cannot point into the mail Sidecar directory, or the reverse.

Advisory members. provenance on a Peer Notice is redundant with the tree and MAY be omitted; if present, it is advisory, and a consumer MUST NOT derive or override the origin class from it. sender_standing, if present, SHOULD be the existing agent-tier value.

section.name: Origin Class Follows the Tree
section.t: Write authority per tree is a behavioral obligation of the same kind as read-only inbound tolerance, single-writer and single-drainer operation, and ingest by copy (): invisible to a document validator, and checked operationally. If it were left to deployments, the separate tree would be decorative, because one writer that chose the tree by inspecting a member would be routing on a member with one level of indirection. The mechanism that enforces it (user identities, mount sets, a host boundary) is out of scope; the property is not, and this section prescribes a check for it.

Connector obligations. The tree a notice is read from is the Runtime's sole assertion of its origin class: inbound/ is mail, and peer/ is same-principal peer origin. A Connector MUST derive the class from the tree, and MUST NOT derive or override it from any member of the document. A document whose kind does not equal the name of the tree it was read from is dropped under the rule of . A Connector that cannot establish which tree a document came from MUST treat it as mail.

The peer tree asserts authenticated origin: a same-principal Agent, reaching this Namespace through a path restricted to authorized peer senders. It asserts nothing about content. Peer content is authored by a peer and unscreened, and may paraphrase external mail (). How a Connector treats each class is out of scope; that it distinguishes the classes only by tree is not. Like the untrusted-content posture of , this obligation protects an Agent from its own inbox, and is stated as a Connector obligation rather than as a property the Runtime relies on. The invariant of is unaffected.

Write-authority partition (Runtime). Write authority over peer/ MUST be distinct from write authority over inbound/. A component that admits messages from a transport not restricted to authorized peer senders (the admitting component, of which a mail deliverer is the usual example) MUST NOT hold write authority over peer/. The restriction MUST be structural, and MUST NOT be configuration that the component reads. The prescribed operational check is a write attempt against peer/ from inside the admitting component, which MUST fail. The rule is one-directional: a component holding peer write authority MAY write inbound/, as the delivery failure notice of requires.

A Runtime MUST NOT write a notice into peer/ on the basis of any claim the message makes about itself. It MAY write there only when the message arrived through a path whose write authority is already restricted to authorized peer senders, or when the message carries a signature that verifies against a configured peer key ().

Verification placement (Runtime). Verification MUST be performed by a component holding peer write authority, which receives candidates through a location that is neither tree (). The admitting component MUST NOT perform verification. A verdict computed by one component and acted on by another would cross a trust boundary as data, which is what this rule keeps out of the decision; and the verifier processes hostile input, so it needs to be the component whose write authority the outcome concerns, not one that parses raw mail.

section.name: Addressing
section.t: A peer address is a bare addr-spec, under the same pattern and exclusions that fixes for draft.to, with no display name. Its local part is the Agent's name within its Runtime, and its domain is the Runtime's authority. A deployment confined to one host, with no mail, MAY use a non-routable domain. Traffic between hosts requires a routable domain, because it travels as mail (). "Routable" means deliverable by the mail system that carries the deployment's peer traffic; the domain need not resolve in the public DNS, because peer keys are configured rather than looked up (). A peer domain MUST belong to exactly one Runtime among those configured as peers, so a deployment that may peer across organizations should use domains it controls. Where an Agent has a bound mailbox (the Binding Record's address, ), the deployment SHOULD use it, so that the Agent has one identity on both lanes.

An addr-spec is used rather than an opaque identifier with a directory, or a URI scheme, because between hosts the transport address is an email address. Any other scheme would need a mapping onto one, and someone to run the mapping. With an addr-spec, the domain names the authority, the peer-key table is keyed by domain, and a signature has something to bind. The grammar, the schema pattern and the header-injection discipline already exist.

Sending needs no new wire shape. A sending Agent writes an ordinary Submit Request () whose draft.to names the peer. The Runtime's recipient policy recognizes a declared edge and routes the request to the peer tree rather than to mail. The Result vocabulary, outbound Sidecars and reply key are the existing ones. Whether a recipient is a peer is Runtime policy, and out of scope, like an allowlist.

message.from on a Peer Notice is authenticated. It is the one from in this protocol that a consumer may treat as authenticated origin: a bare addr-spec, pinned by the schema, and asserted by the Runtime from the restricted write path or from a verified statement (). A Runtime MUST NOT copy it from text the sender supplied. This is the opposite of the rule for mail from (). A Connector's sender check may key on it, because the Runtime asserted it.
A configured peer key vouches only for its own Runtime's domains (). Without this, one Runtime's key could sign a message claiming an address in another Runtime's domain.

One address, one Namespace. A peer address resolves to exactly one Namespace, as every address does in this protocol: one Namespace, one Connector instance, one Agent. Sessions are below the Connector, and this document does not define them.

A peer message is a single unit addressed to one Agent. A Connector MUST NOT cause it to be acted on more than once. A Connector that cannot identify a single target MUST hold the notice rather than fan it out, and SHOULD report the condition through its own side channel ().

"One Agent, one live session; refuse when there are several" is one conformant implementation, not the only one. A finer target (a named session) is out of scope. A coarser one (a pool) is a Runtime alias that expands to several addresses, each resolving to one Namespace, and is not a change to addressing.

section.name: Correlation and Replies
section.t: The peer message id. The sending Runtime mints the peer message id when it accepts the submit. The id MUST be globally unique and unguessable, with at least 128 bits of entropy, and MUST be spelled under the notice_id character set (^[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*$). It has exactly one spelling inside every AMMP document: message.id, message.in_reply_to and message.references[] on a Peer Notice, message_id on a peer-routed Result, and the reply key a sender submits all carry the bare id. When the id is carried in a mail header, it is encoded as <id@domain>, where domain is the domain of the sender's address (). The encoding is applied on the way into the header and removed on the way out, and MUST NOT appear in an AMMP document.

The reverse edge and every ledger depend on two properties of the id: that it is unguessable, and that it has one spelling end to end. Bare 32-character hexadecimal satisfies both, and so does unpadded base64url (subject, between hosts, to ). A mail notice's in_reply_to remains an identifier; the Deliver Notice schema is unchanged.

A reply is a Peer Notice in the reverse direction, on the same tree, correlated with the message it answers. It is not a third kind or a third tree: the tree grants the class, and a reply deserves the class of the message it answers. There is no correlation member; mail threading already provides one, and between hosts it is threading.

table.name: Correlation members on the peer lane

tr.td: MUST equal the peer message id, so that the sender learns it from its own Result. reason_code SHOULD be peer_routed, so that the sender can tell the lanes apart (an open vocabulary, ).
REQUIRED on a reply, and equal to the id being answered. A new task omits it.
How a responder names the message it answers.

section.t: task_id remains an optional, Runtime-minted thread handle ().

Reverse edges. The authorization graph is directed, yet a reply must be able to flow from B to A when only A to B is declared. A Runtime permits a reverse message when its reply key names a peer message in the opposite direction that the Runtime itself issued or placed (at submission, one it placed for the submitting Agent; at reception, one it issued to the replying Agent), within a configured window. This consults a member, but checks it against state the Runtime minted, which is the posture takes for threading: correlation, not trust. Because ids are unguessable, the key is not a forgeable capability. Several replies to one id within the window, and a reply to a reply under the id the Runtime issued for it, are conformant. This document does not fix the window's length; it requires only that the window exists and is configured.

An unresolved reply key is refused, not stripped. A reply key (in_reply_to, or else draft.reply_to_message_id) that the Runtime cannot resolve from its own ledger MUST produce a rejected Result with reason_code unresolved_reply. A Runtime MUST NOT strip the key and route the message on draft.to as a new peer message. A key that resolves but whose reverse edge is not permitted (no declared edge, or an expired window) MUST likewise produce a rejected Result (reason_code peer_reply_window_expired, or the Runtime's own code), and MUST NOT be re-routed. A Peer Notice MUST carry in_reply_to if and only if the placing Runtime resolved it from its own ledger to a peer message id that it issued or placed.

The reason is the reason this profile exists. On the peer lane, a message the sender meant as a reply, which the Runtime quietly turned into a new task, arrives as a new instruction. That is worse than a rejection the sender can act on by resubmitting without the key. The rule is a requirement rather than a permission because a Connector may build policy on it (for example, admitting a replier it would not otherwise accept), and that is sound across a deployment only if every conformant Runtime upholds it. Such a policy MUST NOT widen anything else about the notice's treatment.

Between hosts, the sending Runtime has already rejected an unresolvable key at submission. A verified statement whose in_reply_to the receiving Runtime cannot resolve therefore indicates a stale or forged capability from a configured peer. The receiver MUST NOT place it in peer/ with the key, MUST NOT place it as a new peer task, and MUST log the cause, and it SHOULD tell the sending Runtime with a signed Control Notice (). The ledger binds the participants as well as the id (). The statement is not demoted to mail either: its origin was verified, only its correlation claim failed, and routing it as mail would be a third silent transformation.

Two things called a result. A work result is the responder's content for the requester, described above. A delivery outcome is mechanical feedback from a Connector to its Runtime (delivered, held, and so on). A delivery outcome is not a peer message; it is kept in outbound/ext/<name>/ ().

Delivery failure notices. A Runtime that reports a terminal delivery failure to the sending Agent SHOULD do so as a deliver Notice in the sender's inbound/ tree, with message.from set to the Runtime's own address (amap.router@<domain> or equivalent), in_reply_to set to the peer message id, and a body authored by the Runtime alone. Such a notice MUST NOT be placed in peer/, and MUST NOT quote or forward any text from the receiving Connector's outcome file.

The Runtime is never an allowed peer sender, so this keeps it out of every Connector's peer policy. The mail tree's untrusted-content posture is the right one for "your message did not arrive". And the outcome file is text written by the receiver, so forwarding it would let one Agent put prose in front of another under the Runtime's name. A component holding peer write authority that writes inbound/ is the one direction permits. The peer message id appears in a mail-tree notice, but only to the sender, who already holds it from its own Result, so no capability is disclosed.

section.name: Peer Traffic Between Hosts
section.t: Peer traffic between hosts is mail. The sending Runtime signs it with its own key; there are no per-Agent keys. Traffic on one host needs no signature, because local write permission is a stronger guarantee, although a Runtime MAY sign it too, for a uniform code path, without changing its treatment. A receiving Runtime places a message from another host in peer/ only when every rule in this section holds. Otherwise it hands the message to mail admission, drops it, or refuses it, as specifies.

section.name: The Statement
section.t: The sending Runtime builds a statement, a small JSON object, signs its exact bytes with Ed25519 (), and carries the bytes and the signature in one header field (). The receiver verifies the signature over the bytes it received before parsing them. Nothing is re-serialized: no canonicalization is defined, and whatever serialization the sender chose is the one that is signed.

The peer-statement schema () pins the statement: version v 1, closed at every level, with the members v, key_id, kind ("peer"), id, in_reply_to (optional), from, to, ts, subject, body_sha256 (the digest of the body the receiver will publish), attachments (each with sha256, size_bytes, filename and media_type, in leaf order), sender_exposure (optional, ) and sender_since (optional, ).

Unlike the Runtime-authored notices (), the statement is closed, because it is signed bytes that another Runtime acts on. A member the receiver does not know is a member it cannot bind to what it publishes, and v is the path for evolution. The schema states the shapes. The following rules, which JSON Schema cannot express, are also part of the statement:

li.t: Formats. ts, sender_since and the timestamps in sender_exposure are date-times in UTC, in whole seconds, with the Z designator, and each MUST denote a real instant. Digests are SHA-256 , in lowercase hexadecimal. Every number is a lexical integer, with no fraction and no exponent, so 1.0 is not 1. No string contains an unpaired surrogate ().

Ids. A sending Runtime MUST mint the ids it sends between hosts under ^[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*$, which is the notice_id character set () without ".", with at least 128 bits of entropy, so that <id@domain> is a valid msg-id (). Hexadecimal satisfies this; a base64url id whose first character is "-" MUST be minted again. The statement schema enforces the pattern for id and in_reply_to. An id used only on one host MAY also contain ".", as the notice_id character set allows; an id sent between hosts MUST NOT.
to is one address: a peer message is addressed to one Agent ().

sender_exposure obeys : window_start is not later than window_end; last_external_delivery_ts is present if and only if external_mail_delivered is true, and then lies within the window; and asserted_by is the signing Runtime's configured Runtime address ().
sender_since, when present, is not later than ts.

section.name: Carriage, and the Candidate the Verifier Sees

li.t: s is the statement's bytes, and b is the 64-byte signature over exactly those bytes. Each is base64url without padding ().
k is the statement's key_id, in the clear: the receiver verifies before it parses, so it must choose the key before it can read the statement. The signed key_id MUST equal k.
The field name is matched case-insensitively. The sending Runtime MUST emit exactly one such field.
The sender MUST fold the field so that no line exceeds 998 octets (), and SHOULD fold at 78. It may insert folding whitespace anywhere, because the receiver removes all of it.

A statement MUST NOT exceed 8192 bytes. A sending Runtime that would otherwise emit a larger one SHOULD refuse the submit instead, with a rejected Result whose reason_code is peer_statement_too_large.

The sending Runtime MUST also set Message-ID to <id@domain>, where domain is the domain of from, and SHOULD set In-Reply-To and References to the encoded forms (), so that mail threads coherently and a demoted message still threads as mail.

section.t: The message shape. A sending Runtime SHOULD send either a single text/plain part, or multipart/mixed holding one text/plain part followed by the attachments. The text part SHOULD be charset=utf-8 with base64 transfer encoding, so that transport cannot rewrite it. The sender hashes the UTF-8 encoding of the body after replacing every CRLF pair with LF. Nothing else is normalized: a bare CR, a bare LF, trailing whitespace and a leading dot are all content.
The selection rule. The admitting component reduces a message to a candidate, and the rule is the same at every receiver:

li.t: Leaves. Walk the MIME tree depth-first, descending only into multipart/*. Every other part is a leaf, including message/rfc822, whose octets are its part body as transmitted.
Body. The first leaf of type text/plain whose Content-Disposition is not attachment is the body.
Attachments. Every other leaf, in walk order, is an attachment: a text/html alternative, an inline image, or a second text/plain part.
No body leaf means the empty body.

section.t: A different structure is not forbidden; it is simply likely to fail the attachment count or the body digest, and so to be demoted.
The candidate. The intake location () MUST hold the following, in a layout this document does not prescribe:

li.t: Field bodies. The body of each AMAP-Peer-Statement, AMAP-Peer-Control and Message-ID field, in message order. The admitting component MAY unfold a field body or trim its surrounding whitespace, and MUST NOT otherwise alter it. A field body over 12288 octets MUST be carried as an oversize marker, and MUST NOT be truncated. The 12288-octet limit applies to the field body as transmitted, before unfolding or trimming. A field body the admitting component cannot carry as ASCII text (a non-ASCII octet, or an undecodable value) MUST be carried as an invalid marker in the field's position. A marker keeps the field's identity and multiplicity: the admitting component MUST NOT omit a field, because omitting a second, malformed statement field would leave one well-formed field, and the verifier would select it.
The body leaf, if there is one: its octets after transfer decoding, and the value of its charset parameter, if any.
Each attachment leaf: its octets after transfer decoding, in order.

section.t: The verifier, not the admitting component, decodes the body octets strictly. The charset label, compared case-insensitively, MUST be utf-8 or us-ascii; an absent label means us-ascii. Any other label, or octets that are invalid in the labelled charset, fail check 9 (). The verifier then replaces CRLF pairs with LF and hashes the result, and that same text is what it publishes as body_text.

What is published. On placement, the receiver takes all of the following from the verified statement, and MUST NOT take them from headers: message.id, in_reply_to and from; subject; sender_exposure; and the attachment Descriptors' filename, media_type, size_bytes and sha256. to selects the Namespace. The receiver MUST NOT publish references from headers; it MAY derive them from its own ledger (). The byte sniffing, caps and disposition rules of still apply to the attachment bytes.

Comparisons. Addresses (from, to, the edge graph, the ledger and Runtime addresses) compare the local part exactly and the domain case-insensitively in ASCII. Ids compare exactly, because they are opaque. After unfolding and trimming, Message-ID MUST be exactly "<", the id, "@", the domain and ">", with the id equal to the statement's id and the domain equal to the domain of from.
Logging. A receiver MUST NOT log a raw header field value unescaped. Fields are supplied by the attacker, and k is validated against the key_id pattern before it is used for anything.

section.name: Verification
section.t: The receiver applies these checks in this order. The first one that fails decides the outcome (). Only a candidate that passes every check is eligible for peer/.

li.t: The field. There is exactly one AMAP-Peer-Statement field; with none, the message is not a peer candidate, and is ordinary mail. A message that also carries an AMAP-Peer-Control field is dropped (). The field body is ASCII and is not oversize. With every SP, HTAB, CR and LF removed, it consists of exactly the tags k, s and b, each once, in any order, separated by ";". k matches the key_id pattern. s and b are unpadded base64url; b decodes to 64 bytes, and s to at most 8192.

Known statement. If the SHA-256 digest of the statement bytes equals that of a statement the receiver has recorded and still retains (), the candidate is a duplicate. This check needs no key, and holds whatever else has changed since: a timestamp now outside the window, a key since expired or removed, or a body modified in transit.
Key. k names exactly one configured key, valid at the receiver's clock (not-before ≤ now ≤ not-after, inclusive).
Signature. The signature is valid for that key over the received bytes, under the verification policy of .

Statement. (a) The bytes are UTF-8 without a byte-order mark, and parse as JSON with no repeated member name and no non-JSON constant. They validate against the schema, and key_id equals k. (b) Every rule of that the schema cannot express holds.
Key domain. The domain of from is one of the domains configured for the Runtime that owns the key. A key vouches only for its own Runtime's domains ().
Freshness. ts lies within the window of . While peer admission is closed (no trustworthy bound, ), the window is undefined: the candidate is held in intake, undisposed, until admission reopens.
Exposure asserter. If sender_exposure is present, asserted_by is the configured Runtime address of the Runtime that owns the key.
Body. The body decodes under the charset rule of , and its digest equals body_sha256. The verifier MUST hash bytes it holds itself, and MUST NOT use a digest that the admitting component computed.
Attachments. The count matches; then, for each attachment in order, sha256 and size_bytes match the octets.
Message-ID. There is exactly one such field, matching .
Reservation. No record exists for the pair (the configured Runtime that owns the key, id) (). The candidate is reserved, atomically.

section.t: A reserved candidate is then decided, and the following are not verification failures:

li.t: if to is not hosted here, the candidate is misrouted;
if in_reply_to is present, it must resolve and be permitted ();
otherwise, the receiver's own graph must have the edge from from to to ();
any deployment admission policy is applied ();
otherwise, the decision is placement.

section.t: The decision MUST be persisted on the record before it has any effect (). Only a persisted placement decision is ever published; a persisted refusal or drop MUST NOT be published, whatever happens afterwards.

section.name: Outcomes

table.name: Outcomes for a candidate from another host

tr.td: Every check passes, and the message is routed and permitted.
Check 7 while peer admission is closed (); not yet disposed of.
A failure of check 1 (other than the both-fields drop below), 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 or 11.
An AMAP-Peer-Statement and an AMAP-Peer-Control field in one message ().
Check 2 (a known statement) or check 12 (a known id).

section.t: Mail, demoted. Demotion is a classification, not a delivery. The candidate goes to ordinary mail admission and the deployment's lane policy; where that policy gives the pair no mail lane, it is not delivered. The demoted notice MUST NOT carry sender_exposure, the statement or the signature, and carries the mail-admission verdict the admitting component attached. Mail admission MUST NOT treat an invalid statement as evidence of who sent the message.

Drop and refuse. A dropped or refused candidate is neither placed nor handed to mail admission. Every outcome other than peer and "mail, no statement" MUST be logged with its cause. A refusal is not demoted, because the origin was verified and only an authorization or correlation claim failed; routing it as mail would be a silent transformation ().
Who is told. A Control Notice () MUST be sent only when every one of these holds; a configured k alone is never enough:

li.t: checks 1 to 5(a) passed, so the statement is authenticated by a currently valid configured key and is well-formed enough to name. Before check 4 the sender is unauthenticated, and notifying the claimed sender would be backscatter; between checks 4 and 5(a), the statement cannot be named;
the candidate is a statement, not a Control Notice: nothing is ever sent about a Control Notice ();
the destination is the Runtime address configured for the key's owner, and never an address taken from the message.

section.t: A "dropped, duplicate" notice (check 12) tells the sender that a record with that id already exists. That record's disposition may have been placement or refusal: the notice proves a prior reservation, not that the task failed. Whether and how the sending Agent learns of an outcome is governed by .

section.name: The Replay Store, Windows and Recovery
section.t: Windows. The receiver accepts ts when lower ≤ ts ≤ now + F, both bounds inclusive, where lower = max(H − P, floor):

li.t: F, the allowance for clock skew, defaults to 300 seconds and MUST NOT exceed 900.

P, the past window, defaults to 3600 seconds, and MUST be at least 300 and at most 86400. A message that arrives later than P is demoted, which is visible to the sender. A longer P costs replay storage and a longer key retirement ().

H is the latest receiver time ever observed, kept durably. The lower bound uses H rather than the current clock, so that a clock that steps backwards cannot re-admit a statement whose record has been pruned.
floor is set only by recovery and by window changes, both below.

section.t: Records. Replay identity is scoped to the pair (configured Runtime, id), where the Runtime is the configured peer that owns the verifying key, so that rotating a key never resets it. Each record holds the scope, the id and ts; the SHA-256 digest of the statement bytes; the notice_id minted at reservation; a state, which is reserved, decided or done; and, once decided, the disposition: placement, or a refusal or drop with its cause (and policy_code), and whether a Control Notice is still pending.

Recording. The receiver records a candidate at check 12, after checks 1 to 11 have passed. A candidate that fails any of them records nothing, so a mangled copy cannot suppress the intact one that follows. Misrouted and refused candidates are recorded too, so that their replays are dropped quietly instead of being evaluated again each time. Control Notices () use the same store.
Reservation, decision and effect. These are three durable steps, in order, each atomic:

li.t: Reserve. Check 12 creates the reserved record and mints a fresh notice_id. The candidate stays in the intake location until the record is done. A reservation is undecided, and authorizes nothing.
Decide. The receiver routes, correlates, permits and applies policy (), and persists the disposition on the record, which becomes decided. A refusal or drop also marks its control notice as pending.

Effect. For a placement, the notice is written under the minted notice_id; for a refusal or drop, the Control Notice is durably queued. Only then is the record done. Placement is idempotent: a notice that is already present is not written again.

section.t: A copy that arrives while another copy is reserved or decided matches it at check 2, and is dropped. On restart, the receiver MUST finish every record that is not done, exactly once, by resuming its recorded state, and MUST NOT infer a disposition from the absence of a notice:

li.t: a decided placement is placed if the notice is absent, and is marked done without placing it again if the notice is present;
a decided refusal or drop is not published: its pending control notice is queued, once, and the record is marked done.

section.t: An implementation MUST survive a crash at each of these points: after reservation, after the decision, after a notice is placed, after a control notice is queued, and after a terminal refusal is recorded, including when the graph or policy changed while it was down.

Retention. The receiver MUST retain each done record while H ≤ ts + P, and MAY retain it longer. It MUST NOT prune a record that is not done. A known statement replayed after its retention has lapsed fails freshness, so it is demoted and never placed. Duplicate suppression is therefore effective only within retention: this profile does not promise exactly-once delivery, and an implementation MUST NOT claim it.

Resending. A sending Runtime whose hand-off was ambiguous MAY resend the same id, signed again with a new ts. If the first copy arrived and is retained, the resend is dropped at check 12, and the control notice tells the sender so; if the first copy did not arrive, the resend is placed. A sending Runtime that resends MUST keep the same id, including across a resend that a person approved.

This permission is idempotent only within retention. Once the first copy's record has been pruned, a resend of the same id under a fresh ts finds no record, and is placed a second time. A deployment that cannot accept that MUST forbid signing again in its own deployment profile, and resend only the original bytes, which check 2 drops or freshness demotes. The permission is kept for portability, not as a recommendation.

Recovery. The store and H MUST survive a restart. If the receiver loses the store, or cannot show that a restored store is complete, it MUST restore this barrier: no statement that could already have been accepted under the lost coverage may be admitted again, including at the boundary, under a clock that stepped back, and under the largest F that was ever in effect.

li.t: With H intact, the receiver sets floor to one second after max(C, H) + Fmax, persisted before admission resumes. C is the moment from which it again holds complete evidence, H is the high-water clock at the loss, and Fmax is the largest F in effect at any point that could have admitted a statement still within the lost coverage. Fmax is taken from the retained history of F if that history is provable, and is 900 otherwise. Fmax MUST NOT be chosen from the wall-clock interval ending at C: after a clock rollback, that interval can miss a larger F that was in effect near H. Retaining the largest F ever configured is safe. Any statement accepted before the loss had ts ≤ H + F ≤ max(C, H) + Fmax, so none reaches the floor. The floor is strictly above that bound: an inclusive floor would re-admit a statement accepted at exactly now + F, and C alone would re-admit one accepted before the clock stepped back.

With H lost as well, no trustworthy bound exists, and the receiver MUST close peer admission: candidates reaching check 7 are held in intake, and nothing is placed or demoted on a window the receiver cannot define. Admission reopens only when the operator records a bound B that is at or after the largest receiver time before the loss. The floor is then one second after B + Fmax, with Fmax determined as above: losing H does not by itself lose the history of F. The held candidates are then evaluated in arrival order. The current wall-clock time is not a bound.

section.t: Window changes. Narrowing P or F takes effect at once. Widening P MUST NOT re-admit anything: the receiver sets the floor to the lower bound in effect at the moment of the change, and the window then widens only as records accumulate.

section.name: Correlation and Edges Between Hosts
section.t: The ledger. A Runtime keeps a record for every peer message it issued to another host or placed. Each record holds the id; the local Agent and the remote Agent; the direction (issued or placed); and an expiry, the configured reply window (). The ledger is scoped to peer messages: a mail notice id never resolves.

Resolution. A verified statement carrying in_reply_to resolves only if a record exists whose id equals in_reply_to, whose local Agent equals to, whose remote Agent equals from, and which has not expired. Possession of an id is not authority: an id presented by another Agent on the same host, or by any Agent on another host, does not resolve.

Permission. A resolved reply to a record this Runtime issued is a reverse message, and is permitted without an edge (). A resolved message against a record this Runtime placed is a follow-up in the same direction, and needs the edge from from to to. A statement without in_reply_to needs the edge.

The receiver's own graph. The edge MUST be checked against the receiver's own graph. The sending Runtime checked its edge at submission (), but which peers may task an Agent is the receiving Runtime's decision. If correlation fails, the outcome is "refuse: unresolved reply"; if permission fails, it is "refuse: no edge". Neither is demoted.

At submission. The sending Runtime MUST apply the same binding: a reply key resolves only if the submitting Agent is the record's local Agent. It SHOULD also refuse at submission a message it already knows the receiver will refuse, such as one for a pair it knows has no edge or is held by policy, so that the Agent learns of it at once. The receiver remains the authority.

section.name: Keys
section.t: Configuration. The operator configures, at every receiver, each peer Runtime's domain set, its Runtime address (amap.router@<domain> or equivalent), and its key set. Trust anchors are configured, not discovered: there is no DNS publication, directory or certificate chain. A receiver MUST refuse to load a configuration in which:

li.t: a key_id occurs twice, across all peers (the receiver selects a key by k alone);
a not-before time is later than its not-after time;
a public key is not a canonical encoding of a curve point; or
a public key is of small order.

section.t: A sending Runtime SHOULD make its key ids globally unique, for example by deriving them from a fingerprint of the public key.

These are configuration-time checks, a gate separate from verification. A bare Ed25519 implementation will construct and verify under a small-order or non-canonical key; the key loader, not the verifier, is what refuses one. An implementation MUST demonstrate the refusal through its loader, and MUST NOT count passing the vectors marked for rejection at verification as covering it.
Rotation. A receiver MUST support at least two concurrent keys per peer. A rotation proceeds as follows:

li.t: Add the new key at every receiver.
Switch the sender to it.
If the sender stops using the old key at time T, receivers keep the old key valid until at least T + F + P, because a statement signed at T can carry a ts up to T + F, and arrive up to P after that.

section.t: Validity is inclusive at both ends. Revocation is removing a key or ending its validity. Replay records are scoped to the Runtime rather than the key, so neither retiring nor revoking a key erases replay evidence ().

The signing key is a Runtime credential (). It MUST NOT be readable from any Agent Namespace or by the admitting component. It MUST NOT be used to sign anything except this profile's statements and Control Notices, which their kind members keep apart.

Verification policy. Verification is Ed25519 as specified in , with the cofactorless equation [S]B = R + [k]A. A verifier MUST reject a signature whose S is not less than L; a non-canonical encoding of R or A; and a key that failed the configuration checks above. A point encoding MUST be decoded canonically before any other check is applied to it: the "negative zero" encoding of x = 0 (y = p − 1 with the sign bit set) is non-canonical, and is rejected as such before a small-order check is reached.

This document requires nothing about how Ed25519 is computed. A vetted library, a system binary or any other implementation conforms if it produces these results. The conformance suite holds the test vectors of (TEST 1 to 3), and negative vectors marked for rejection either at verification or at configuration (). An implementation MUST pass both kinds through the implementation it ships.

section.name: Control Notices
section.t: A receiving Runtime tells a configured sending Runtime what it did with a statement it did not place, using a signed Control Notice. The peer-control schema () pins it: version v 1, closed, with the members v, key_id, kind ("control"), id, from, to, ts, about, outcome, cause, and policy_code (with cause policy).

Form. A Control Notice is carried in an AMAP-Peer-Control header field with the k, s and b grammar of , signed with the same per-Runtime key. Its kind makes it impossible to read as a peer statement, and the reverse. It carries no free text: the cause vocabulary is closed, and the receiving Runtime composes any words itself. It travels as mail between Runtime addresses.

When. A receiver SHOULD send one for every outcome marks, and MUST send one only when the eligibility conditions of hold in full: never for a failure before check 5(b), never for a duplicate caught at check 2, never about a Control Notice, and never merely because a key was found. There is one notice per record: the pending notice is part of the record's disposition (), MUST be queued durably before the record is done, and MUST be sent at most once, including across a crash. A receiver MAY rate-limit Control Notices; any suppression MUST be logged.
policy_code is defined by the deployment. A receiving Runtime renders a description it defines locally. An unknown token gets a generic description, and MUST NOT be interpreted.

Addressing. from is the receiver's own Runtime address. to MUST be the Runtime address configured for the peer that owns the verifying key, and MUST NOT be an address taken from the message. A control notice MUST NOT be sent to a Runtime that is not a configured peer.

Receiving one. A Runtime applies checks 1 to 5 of , with AMAP-Peer-Control and the control schema in place of the statement's. It then requires all of these: from is the Runtime address of the peer that owns the key; to is its own Runtime address; ts is fresh (); the notice's pair (Runtime, id) is new; and about names a ledger record that this Runtime issued to an Agent in the signer's domains.

What it does. It SHOULD give the issuing Agent a failure notice authored by the Runtime in inbound/ (the delivery failure notice of ), with no text from the Control Notice except the vocabulary values. Where it does, the failure notice is owed from the moment the record is reserved, and the record is done only once the failure notice is durable; a crash in between is finished by recovery, once.

One per message. An issued record receives at most one failure notice. A later Control Notice about the same about, under a different id, is dropped. A "dropped, duplicate" report means that a record for the message exists at the receiver, whose disposition may have been placement; it is not proof that the task failed.
Failures. A Control Notice that fails any rule is dropped and logged: it MUST NOT be placed, handed to mail admission, or answered. A message carrying both fields is dropped.

section.name: Optional: Sender Age, and Deployment Admission Policy
section.t: A deployment MAY refuse authenticated peer messages for reasons of its own, such as a first-sight quarantine for a new sender, or a requirement that every delegation between hosts carry sender_exposure. The refusal is "refuse: policy", with a policy_code defined by the deployment. The policies themselves are the deployment's business, not this profile's.
Measuring a sender's age at the receiver, from first sight, would make every Agent's first delegation to each host fail. The optional signed member sender_since exists to avoid that:

li.t: It is the time at which the sending Runtime first enrolled the sending Agent's identity, as that Runtime defines identity, taken from its durable registry.
It is a Runtime assertion, covered by the signature, and MUST NOT be taken from text the sender supplied.

It has the format of ts, and is not later than ts. Skew is absorbed by the age itself: a receiver measures age as its own clock minus sender_since, so a few minutes of skew change nothing under a policy measured in hours.

Continuity. The sending Runtime MUST NOT reset it for a continuation of the same identity: a restart, a rebinding, a re-creation or a key rotation keeps the value. A new enrollment of the identity starts a new value. The sending Runtime decides which of the two a given event is, and MUST decide it the same way every time for that identity.

Consistency. A receiver that enforces a sender-age policy MUST keep the last value it accepted for each pair (Runtime, from). A later statement that asserts an earlier value claims an older enrollment than the Runtime previously asserted; it is inconsistent, and the receiver refuses it with its own policy_code. A later value is a new enrollment, and the age starts again.

section.t: A receiver MAY enforce a minimum sender age from it. Its absence means "not asserted", and a receiver MUST NOT read it as "new" or as "old enough". A deployment that requires it refuses its absence with its own policy_code.

section.name: The Intake Location
section.t: The intake location is REQUIRED, as a structural property with no prescribed layout. A message admitted from a shared transport that presents as a peer or control candidate MUST be held, until it is disposed of, in a location that is neither inbound/ nor peer/, that is writable by the admitting component and readable by the verifying component, and that is unreachable from any Agent Namespace. Candidates MUST be held as the candidate of : the verifier MUST NOT parse mail. The verifier MUST apply the read-side discipline of to candidates, since the admitting component is less trusted than the verifier. The verifier disposes of each candidate exactly once: it places it in peer/, minting the notice_id at reservation (); or it hands it to mail admission, which, if it delivers, places it in inbound/ under a notice_id minted there; or it drops or refuses it, logging the cause. A candidate held while peer admission is closed () is not yet disposed of, and stays in the intake location until admission reopens.

How a Runtime divides its intake (one location or several, for example by candidate kind), and where it keeps the traffic it authors itself, are implementation choices; this section constrains only the properties above.

section.name: Sender Exposure
section.t: The split between Runtime assertions and sender claims () applies: disposition, verdict and sender_standing are Runtime assertions, while subject and body_text (and, on the mail tree, from) are sender claims. An exposure record belongs on the assertion side. It records delivery, not reading: a Runtime can know that it delivered external mail to the sender's Namespace, but cannot know what the sender did with it.
A Peer Notice asserting exposure, with the stamp in message.sender_exposure:

figure.name: fixtures/valid/peer-exposure-true.json
figure.sourcecode: { "contract_version": "2", "notice_id": "7b2a1c0d9e8f47a6b5c4d3e2f1a0b9c8", "ts": "2026-09-03T12:05:00Z", "kind": "peer", "message": { "id": "7b2a1c0d9e8f47a6b5c4d3e2f1a0b9c8", "from": "triage@fleet.example", "subject": "Customer asks for an export", "preview": "A customer mail this morning asks whether", "mailbox": "peer", "sender_exposure": { "asserted_by": "amap.router@fleet.example", "external_mail_delivered": true, "window_start": "2026-09-02T12:05:00Z", "window_end": "2026-09-03T12:05:00Z", "last_external_delivery_ts": "2026-09-03T08:41:10Z", "derived_from": ["1721457600000000001-4242"] } } }

li.t: Placement. It is a member of message, beside sender_standing, provenance and verdict, so that the Runtime's assessments of the message are kept together. The schema requires asserted_by (a bare addr-spec naming the asserting Runtime; between hosts, the signer), external_mail_delivered, window_start and window_end, and requires last_external_delivery_ts when the boolean is true. Its absence when the boolean is false is stated here, not in the schema.

Shape. A boolean over an explicit window, plus the most recent timestamp. There is no count, because a count would assert a precision that a measure of delivery lacks. derived_from is optional, and present only where the Runtime observed the derivation itself (the sender's reply key named a notice in its mail tree).

Absence means "not assessed". A consumer MUST NOT read the member's absence as "no exposure". false, asserted, is a stronger statement than the member omitted: it says that the Runtime assessed the window and delivered no external mail. A Runtime that is the only writer of a sender's mail tree, and has written there only same-principal Agent mail and its own delivery failure notices, SHOULD assert false. Notices the Runtime authors in the mail tree (the delivery failure notices of ) are not external mail, and MUST NOT make the boolean true. Moving window_start forward to the moment the Runtime's assessment began (for example, an instance's approval time after a reset) keeps the window on the wire equal to the span assessed.

Not settable by the sender. On one host, the Submit Request envelope is closed (), so a request carrying the member is rejected, which is stronger than stripping it. Between hosts, it is taken only from the verified statement, and is removed on demotion (). A Runtime MUST NOT accept it from any sender.
Use. It MUST NOT drive routing or treatment (). It is advisory, for audit, and covered by the signature.

section.t: Lineage declared by the sender is not included. Such a member would ride on the Submit Request, whose envelope is closed, so adding it would be a major change; it would work only when the sender cooperates, which is the case where it is least needed; and a forgeable member invites readers to trust it. Most of its value is recovered without one: when a sender's reply key names a notice in its mail tree, the Runtime knows which external message the peer message derives from, and records that as its own observation (derived_from, and the audit log).

section.name: Delivery Outcomes, Retention, Deletion and Presentation

li.t: Delivery outcomes are not a profile artifact. A Connector that reports what it did with a notice (delivered, held, refused, and so on) writes the report under outbound/ext/<name>/, in a shape agreed out of band with its Runtime, under the stable Connector id that requires. carries the one normative rule: an outcome is a claim by the receiving side, never proof of delivery or of non-delivery, and the Runtime's own delivery record is authoritative over it (). If a second Connector needs outcomes, that is the point at which to define a shape for them in this profile.

Retention. The record is the audit log, not the spool. The Runtime logs every candidate it disposes of (id, from, to, tree, exposure, signature verdict, and any demotion or refusal cause) to the per-Agent audit/log.jsonl it owns, and to its own store of record. Spool retention for peer/ follows the mail row of the deletion table () unchanged.
Deletion rights. The deletion table () applies to peer/ artifacts exactly as to inbound ones: written by the Runtime, and deleted by the Runtime only.

Presentation. A Connector presenting a peer body MUST meet the presentation obligations of , with one prohibition and two additions. It MUST NOT convey that the sender is unauthenticated: on this tree, message.from is asserted by the Runtime from the restricted write path (), and saying otherwise contradicts the mechanism the tree exists to provide. It SHOULD convey that an authenticated request is still bounded by what the receiving Agent is authorized to do: a verified sender can ask for something the receiver may not perform, and a framing that reads as a grant invites the reader to treat verified identity as having settled that question. It SHOULD convey that authenticated origin is not a warranty about content: peer content is authored by a peer and unscreened, and may paraphrase external mail (). Authenticated who; unverified what.

None of this is an enforcement mechanism. Enforcement on this tree is the write-authority partition and the origin-follows-the-tree rule (); presentation is what a Connector states to a reader who can ignore it. The reason to get it right is that the alternative asserts something false.

section.name: Versioning
section.t: The fail-closed rule. contract_version is a major-version string. A consumer that reads a higher major than it speaks MUST fail closed — refuse to process the artifact — and MUST NOT silently mis-parse it.

Version-check ordering. A consumer MUST implement the version check by reading contract_version before any schema validation, comparing majors as non-negative decimal integers. An absent major, a lower major, or a higher major is a version refusal: fail closed, as a distinct, logged outcome, never folded into the malformed-document drop path of .

Checking the version first is what makes fail-closed implementable at all. A validator that runs schema checks first cannot distinguish "wrong version" from "malformed," and a strict schema would reject a future-major document for the wrong reason entirely.

This ordering rule is about inbound artifacts a Connector consumes, which have no mechanism in this protocol to carry a distinct outcome back to the Runtime. It does not reach the outbound direction: a Runtime version-refusing a Submit Request MAY carry that refusal on the ordinary request-rejection path — a top-level rejected Result with reason_code: "unsupported_contract_version" () — and, per the conformance classes below, MUST do so for the version-absent request fixture. That is still a distinct, legible outcome rather than a fold into the malformed-request case: reason_code is exactly this protocol's mechanism for saying why a rejected fired, and a consumer MUST already tolerate a reason_code it does not otherwise interpret. A Runtime has no equivalent document to write for a version-refused Notice it never emits — hence the asymmetry: logged-only inbound, rejected outbound.

A version signal, not member rejection, is the boundary. Rejecting a document because it carries an unrecognized member is not a version mechanism. Under closed envelopes, a consumer that meets a new member rejects the whole document: inbound, that is silent loss of the message; outbound, it is an accidental schema error rather than a designed refusal. And while the version string is unchanged, nothing can react to the new member. A change that a consumer of the current wire major would reject or misread as a whole document therefore requires a new wire major, so that the consumer refuses it by version, legibly, and both sides upgrade deliberately. Schema strictness and protocol version are separate axes, and this document does not use the first as the second.
Unknown-member tolerance is direction-aware. The rule is stated per direction because the two directions have opposite threat models.

li.t: Runtime-authored artifacts — Deliver Notice, Inbound Message, Result, Peer Notice — are open. A consumer MUST ignore members it does not recognize, at every level of the document, and MUST NOT reject, drop, or fail the artifact on their account. Strictness in this direction defends nothing: the producer is trusted by construction, and in the one posture where an attacker can author a Notice — a writable inbound tree — that attacker can author a fully schema-valid one, so strictness is not the defense there. Its failure mode is silent loss of mail. Emitting an unknown member is still a producer non-conformance: a Runtime MUST NOT emit members this document does not define. In the schemas, additionalProperties: false is absent from the deliver-notice, inbound-message, result and peer-notice schemas at every level — top level, message, Descriptor items, and attestation — while the clean-gating conditionals are orthogonal and remain.

The Submit Request envelope is closed, additionalProperties: false at every level. Closure does real security work there: it is what bars an outbound content_ref and any other smuggled member; the validator is the trusted Runtime; and a refusal is a legible, per-request rejected Result, never a silent loss. A Runtime MUST reject a request carrying unrecognized members.
Consequently: adding an optional member to a Runtime-authored artifact is additive and needs no new wire major; adding any member to the Submit Request requires one.

The Binding Record is closed, for the separate reason given in . The signed Peer Statement and Control Notice are closed because they are signed bytes another Runtime acts on (); they carry their own version member, v.

section.t: Tolerance extends to values, not only members. An optional, explicitly advisory enum on a Runtime-authored artifact — message.sender_standing and message.provenance () — is scoped the same way. A consumer MUST tolerate a value it does not recognize, treating it as opaque or as the member being absent, and MUST NOT reject, drop, or fail the artifact on that account; a Runtime MAY add a value to either vocabulary without a new wire major. Without this, a Runtime adding a new sender_standing or provenance value would silently lose every Notice carrying it, against every Connector still validating the old enum — the member case again, at the value level. In the schemas, the enum constraint is absent from these two members.

This is not a universal loosening of every enum. kind, outcome — both the top-level Result outcome and the per-attachment outcome — and the inbound Descriptor's disposition remain closed, enum-locked vocabularies. kind and outcome gate which processing path a document takes at all, and disposition gates byte publication (), so a new value in any of them is a behavioral fork a consumer cannot safely treat as opaque. Introducing one requires a new wire major.

When the wire major changes, and when it does not. The wire major exists to force a legible, fail-closed refusal where a whole document that a counterpart already accepts would otherwise be silently misread or silently dropped. A change whose only incompatibility already travels a designed, legible, per-artifact refusal path (a rejected Result for one request, or the drop of one Notice under ) does not require one. Changing the major for such a change would make every counterpart on the old major refuse all traffic, including traffic the change does not affect, which is the failure the major exists to prevent. Revisions of this document are not wire versions: a revision that requires no new wire major leaves contract_version unchanged.

Why the wire version is "2". The wire version starts at "2", not "1", because the value "1" is already taken. Before this document, implementations exchanged an earlier, incompatible shape under "1": it had no attachments, and its envelopes were closed. Reusing "1" for this document's shapes would give one major two incompatible meanings, and would defeat the fail-closed rule above exactly where it is needed: a consumer of the old shape would accept a document it cannot process. "2" is also what current implementations emit and check. records the history. The authors would be glad of the community's view on whether a reset is nonetheless worth its cost.

Change control. A capability change starts with a change to this document, its schemas, and its fixtures, before either side implements it. Neither a Runtime nor a Connector may invent a wire member locally. A change that breaks an existing fixture is taken deliberately by both sides, and requires a new wire major only under the rule above.

The rest of this table reflects what implementations emit today; specified-but-unbuilt enrichment stays optional, and tightening any of it to required would be a future major bump.
